title: Treaties of Hard Labour and Lochaber
summary: In 1768 and 1770 the Cherokee ceded land to Virginia at Hard Labour and Lochaber; surveyor John Donelson's 1771 line swung west to the Kentucky River.
bodyMarkdown:
In 1768 Britain was trying to draw a line between its colonies and Native land. The Proclamation of 1763 had closed the country west of the mountains to settlers, but squatters, hunters, and land companies kept pushing. Two sets of talks that fall tried to fix the boundary. In the north, the Iroquois met Sir William Johnson at the [Treaty of Fort Stanwix](/stories/treaty-of-fort-stanwix-1768/). In the south, the Cherokee met the British superintendent for the southern Indians, [John Stuart](/people/#john-stuart).

Stuart met Cherokee headmen at Hard Labour Creek in South Carolina. The [treaty text](https://encyclopediavirginia.org/primary-documents/the-treaty-of-hard-labor-october-14-1768/) is dated October 14, 1768. It drew a line from Chiswell's lead mine in southwest Virginia to the mouth of the Kanawha, at today's Point Pleasant, West Virginia. That put both banks of the Kanawha inside Virginia.

Virginia wanted more. Two years later, at Lochaber, South Carolina, on October 18, 1770, the Cherokee ceded still more land and agreed that the line would be run on the ground.

Surveyor [John Donelson](/people/#john-donelson) walked the line in 1771, with the Cherokee leader [Attakullakulla](/people/#attakullakulla) along. He did not run it to the Kanawha. He ran it west to the mouth of the [Kentucky River](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kentucky_River), then often called the Louisa. That swing added roughly ten million acres to Virginia's side, much of eastern Kentucky among them. Historians still argue over whether the Cherokee understood the change or were paid for it.

The Cherokee were not the only people with a stake. Shawnee hunters who actually used the Bluegrass did not sign Hard Labour, Lochaber, or Fort Stanwix. They fought for that country at Point Pleasant in 1774, and the [Treaty of Camp Charlotte](/stories/treaty-of-camp-charlotte-1774/) followed.

These lines mattered. They gave Virginia a paper claim, and surveyors like [Hancock Taylor](/people/#hancock-taylor) and land men like [Richard Henderson](/people/#richard-henderson) were soon at work in Kentucky.

## Kentucky today

The Donelson line has no monument in Kentucky. Its western end, the mouth of the Kentucky River, is at Carrollton, where General Butler State Resort Park sits above the meeting of the Kentucky and the Ohio.
